summary: The Tao Te Ching is a collection of 81 short sections attributed to Laozi and dated by Standard Ebooks to about the 6th century BC. This edition uses the English translation by James Legge. The sections speak in compact, paradoxical lines about the Tao, the way that cannot be fully named, and about how a ruler or an ordinary person should act in line with it. Water, softness, small beginnings and restraint recur as images, and each section can be read alone in a minute.
context: The oldest excavated pieces are the Guodian bamboo slips, from about 300 BCE, found in 1993 near Guodian in Hubei. The Mawangdui silk texts, from a tomb dated 168 BCE and opened in 1973, put the Te section before the Tao section. Later readers worked through commentary editions, among them those of Heshang Gong and Wang Bi. Sima Qian tells of Laozi as an archivist who wrote the book for a gatekeeper at the Han-ku Pass. The text was first translated into French in the early 19th century.

ideas.title: The Tao cannot be named
ideas.note: Section I opens by saying that the Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring Tao, and the name that can be named is not the enduring name.

ideas.title: Water as the model
ideas.note: Section VIII praises water for benefiting all things without contest.

ideas.title: Small beginnings
ideas.note: Section LXIV says the tree that fills the arms grew from a tiny sprout.

ideas.title: Softness outlasts hardness
ideas.note: Section LXXVI sets the supple and weak of living things against the stiff and strong of the dead.

ideas.title: Three things to hold
ideas.note: Section LXVII lists three precious things the speaker prizes and holds fast.

passages.quote: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.
passages.why: Opening line of the whole book and its best-known claim about language.

passages.quote: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
passages.why: Water is the book's favorite picture of effortless goodness.

passages.quote: Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long. The reason why heaven and earth are able to endure and continue thus long is because they do not live of, or for, themselves. This is how they are able to continue and endure.
passages.why: Explains endurance through not living for oneself.

passages.quote: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step. He who acts (with an ulterior purpose) does harm; he who takes hold of a thing (in the same way) loses his hold.
passages.why: Shows the principle of patient, small starts.

passages.quote: I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others. With that gentleness I can be bold; with that economy I can be liberal; shrinking from taking precedence of others, I can become a vessel of the highest honour.
passages.why: A compact statement of the speaker's own practice.

passages.quote: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. (So it is with) all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
passages.why: Argues for softness from the contrast of life and death.
